new_statements.quote: Stress and intonation appear to be closely related. A full analysis has not yet been attempted. However it has been observed that a primary (or word) stress tends to fall on the last of a two or three syllable sequence.
new_statements.citation: Rodda, Rosemary. 1961. Phonemes of Batak. Philippine Journal of Science 90(2): 259-262.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., text layer present; = pp. 121-124 of from archive.org item philippine-journal-of-science_1961-06_90_2, which carries no access-restricted flag and downloads directly) and viewed the page image. Footnote 3 on p. 259 reads exactly: "Stress and intonation appear to be closely related. A full analysis has not yet been attempted. However it has been observed that a primary (or word) stress tends to fall on the last of a two or three syllable sequence." (the scanned renders the footnote marker as a degree sign; the image shows superscript 3, attached to "three classes of phonemes" in the body). Same text appears in the issue scanned (djvu line 6238) and extracted text (line 4899).…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (word) stress tends to fall on the last syllable of a two- or three-syllable word/sequence, i.e. final stress; the author flags this as a preliminary observation (no full analysis) and says stress is closely tied to intonation. Stress is not marked in her phonemic transcription (she uses the grave accent only for a pre-glottal-stop vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('tends to'). Later evidence points the other way: Zorc's review of Thiessen (p. 109) reports that Warren 1959 lists Batak accent minimal pairs (dato 'that' : dató 'chief') while Zorc's own Batak data show accent differences that are idiolectal and due to Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata; Thiessen 1981:10 (via Zorc) says accent is not contrastive in any Palawan variety and is not written.
new_statements.domain_note: Author calls it 'primary (or word) stress' but describes it over 'a two or three syllable sequence' and ties it to intonation; domain is the word in citation/text forms, with possible phrase-level conditioning. Data: monolingual fieldwork, east-coast Palawan Batak, 1956-1959.
new_statements.identity_note: Rodda 1961 describes the Batak of the east coast of Palawan (area extending c. 40 miles north of latitude 10 degrees), fieldwork 1956-1959, no dialect named; this is bata1301 [bya] (Palawan Batak), not any Sumatran Batak language. Lobel 2013:86 notes each Batak community (e.g. Roxas, Puerto Princesa) has its own dialect. Zorc's review (Batak field data) and Thiessen 1981 (via Zorc) suggest accent is non-contrastive / idiolectal, so the catalog entry should carry Rodda's hedge.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. [c. 1982-84]. Review of Thiessen, Henry Arnold, 1981, Phonological reconstruction of Proto-Palawan (Anthropological Papers 10, Manila: National Museum). pp. 109-111 (offprint 044, zorc.net).
sources.note: p. 109: quotes Thiessen 1981:10 that word accent in the South Palawan dialects falls on one of the last two syllables and 'In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written'; Zorc adds that Warren 1959 lists Batak accent minimal pairs (dato 'that' : dató 'chief') but that his own Aborlan, Brooke's Point and Batak data 'indicate that accent differences are the result of Tagalog or Bisayan superstrata and often differ from one idiolect to another'; Proto-Palawan probably lost PPH accent
